title: The 1947 wave, the Twining memo and Project Sign, 1947-49
notes: Appendix T's wave-1947 merged in: Kenneth Arnold has two edges on the board, too thin for a topic of its own. The green fireballs of 1948-49 sit here as the other Air Force study of the period.

lead.text: In September 1947 Lt. Gen. Nathan Twining of Air Materiel Command wrote that the flying disc phenomenon was something real, and his letter led to Project SIGN. SIGN's staff wrote a classified Estimate of the Situation in 1948 calling the objects interplanetary; the Air Force Chief of Staff rejected it for lacking proof, and copies were destroyed.

summary.text: The wave that prompted it began with Kenneth Arnold's sighting in the Cascades on 24 June 1947, which produced an Army Air Forces investigative file that survives. The name flying saucer is traced, by the Condon Report's reconstruction of the wire coverage, to the press's paraphrase of how he said the objects moved, not of their shape.

Twining's memorandum of 23 September 1947 went to Brig. Gen. George Schulgen of Air Force intelligence requirements, who five weeks later issued a collection memorandum telling intelligence collectors what to look for in flying saucer type aircraft.

SIGN was directed on 30 December 1947 and hosted by Air Materiel Command intelligence at Wright Field. After its Estimate was rejected it became Project GRUDGE on 11 February 1949, and GRUDGE was renamed Blue Book in March 1952.
The same years brought the green fireballs, investigated from Albuquerque by the University of New Mexico meteoriticist Lincoln LaPaz and taken up at a conference at Los Alamos on 16 February 1949.

record.text: Twining's memorandum, AMC Opinion Concerning Flying Discs, signed as commander of Air Materiel Command, states: "The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious." It asks that consideration be given to the possibility that the objects are of domestic origin, the product of some high security project unknown to Air Force intelligence or to AMC.
The Condon Report records that Twining's letter directed the establishment of a study of UFOs, which received priority designation in December 1947 and began as Project SIGN.

Schulgen's memorandum, Intelligence Requirements on Flying Saucer Type Aircraft, is dated 28 October 1947 and was distributed on 30 October. It directs collectors to report on "extreme maneuverability and apparent ability to almost hover", a relatively flat bottom with extreme light-reflecting ability, and an oval or disc plan form with a dome.

The same memorandum lists nuclear propulsion among the systems to investigate, frames the objects as possibly manned aircraft of Russian origin derived from the German Horten brothers' designs, and asks where the Hortens now are.
A letter of 24 November 1947 from Air Materiel Command intelligence to the Air Force Chief of Staff on the flying disc problem survives as a scan.

The Condon Report records that staff members prepared a classified Estimate of the Situation in July 1948 asserting that UFOs were interplanetary vehicles, that the Chief of Staff, Gen. Hoyt Vandenberg, rejected it for lacking proof, and that copies were destroyed.

GRUDGE's report put UFO reports down to misinterpretation of conventional objects, mass hysteria, hoaxes or psychological factors, found no direct threat to national security, and recommended reducing the investigation; the board notes that SIGN became GRUDGE months after the Estimate was destroyed.
SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book were all hosted at Wright-Patterson under Air Materiel Command intelligence and its successor ATIC.

Los Alamos National Laboratory states that the 16 February 1949 green fireballs conference was attended by its director Norris Bradbury, Frederick Reines and Edward Teller with FBI, Atomic Energy Commission and military representatives, that its National Security Research Center holds the minutes, and that the conference ultimately dismissed the fireballs as a significant national security threat.

The laboratory also says its research center does not appear to hold materials on Project Twinkle, the later green fireball observation effort, though not every item in its collections is searchable, and that it receives several UFO-related FOIA requests a year.

The Fourth Air Force's 1947 index carries correspondence to and from Arnold, including an investigation of his report sent to the AAF and ADC on 18 July 1947 and a request of 22 July 1947 from R. A. Palmer of Ventura Press for an article on flying saucers.

claimed.text: Edward Ruppelt, Blue Book's first director, first published the Estimate's existence, content and destruction in his 1956 book, from his time in charge of the files; the Condon Report later recorded the same.

Ruppelt's account also has SIGN operating under Air Materiel Command intelligence with J. Allen Hynek retained as its scientific consultant from 1948, and has Kirtland intelligence officers calling in LaPaz, who concluded the fireballs did not behave as meteors would.

The board carries, at Tier 2, that Project Twinkle, a network of observation and photographic stations, was set up in December 1949 but never fully implemented, and that newly declassified records of the 1949 conference were reported in the press in July 2026.

Jesse Michels said in October 2025 that LaPaz and Clyde Tombaugh led a military-funded search for small natural satellites of the Earth from 1953, and that Aviation Week published a LaPaz statement on two objects in orbit in August 1954. Neither the search nor the magazine issue has been opened by the board, so both are the speaker's account.

On the board's reading, a collection requirement that asks about atomic propulsion does not fit a genuine belief that the objects were Soviet flying wings, and the Horten framing worked as a collection cover story. That is the board's inference from the two memoranda read in sequence.

The board also infers that Twining's reference to a high security project unknown to his command shows awareness in 1947 of compartments above the Air Force's own technical intelligence chain, that GRUDGE's conclusions read as a corrective to the destroyed Estimate, and that the destruction is the earliest instance of adverse records vanishing without authority.

The board infers that Howard McCoy's AMC intelligence organisation did the staff work behind Twining's memorandum, and that AMC's 1947 to 1949 intelligence files are the most likely surviving custody record for any recovered materiel; no comprehensive review of them has been reported.

contested.text: Air Force representatives and Rep. L. Mendel Rivers have asserted that no Estimate ever existed. The board favours the Air Force's own contracted report, written with access to its files, over those public denials; that weighing is its inference.
Twining's memorandum itself, in the standard declassified text, records that the lack of physical evidence in the form of crash-recovered exhibits constrained AMC's analysis.
The Estimate's rejection was on the ground that it lacked proof, and GRUDGE, the project that replaced SIGN, found the reports explained by misinterpretation, mass hysteria and hoaxes.

AARO's 2024 historical report concludes that most sightings across the legacy programmes, SIGN among them, were ordinary objects and misidentification, and that no official review has ever confirmed extraterrestrial technology.
The green fireballs conference itself dismissed the fireballs as a significant national security threat.

questions: Does any copy of the 1948 Estimate of the Situation survive, and who ordered the destruction of the others?
Was Twining's trip to New Mexico of 7 July 1947 connected with the Roswell recovery? No itinerary has been released.
What does the 24 November 1947 letter from AMC intelligence to the Chief of Staff actually say? The scan has never been transcribed.
Have Air Materiel Command's T-2 intelligence files for 1947 to 1949 ever been reviewed for declassification, and where are they now?
What do the minutes of the February 1949 Los Alamos conference record, and where did the Project Twinkle records go?
What did Aviation Week publish from LaPaz in August 1954, if anything?
